articles.text: The City of Piedmont received an ‘AAA’ long-term rating from Standard & Poor’s (S&P) Global Ratings, the highest possible rating issued by the credit rating agency. Cities that receive this rating are considered to have the highest degree of safety regarding timely servicing of financial obligations and to have the lowest credit risk. S&P assigned the long-term rating to the city’s proposed $19.5 million bond series for the new community pool. The credit rating agency noted Piedmont’s “very strong local economy, reflected in the city’s mature residential base, very high resident incomes, and access to diverse employment in the San Francisco Bay Area,” according to its accompanying document. The city also exhibited “historical maintenance of very strong reserves and liquidity, good financial management, and use of multiyear budget forecasting,” the S&P ratings document stated. The rating will allow the city to sell the bonds at lower interest rates. The bonds will be sold on November 18, and interest on bonds is tax-exempt with maturities ranging from 2023 through 2051. Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King acknowledged the significance of the credit rating when speaking at a community pool town hall hosted by the League of Women Voters (LWV) on November 4. “We were just granted a AAA credit rating, which is just extraordinary,” Mayor King said. “It’s going to result in tremendous savings for our city as we pursue this project.” Mayor King also noted that the city has never issued general obligation bonds, so this is the first credit rating issued to the city. Bonds will be available in $5,000 denominations. Community members interested in purchasing the bonds may contact Bank of America Securities at 510-208-3850. articles.text: The Piedmont Turkey Trot took a hiatus last year due to COVID-19 restrictions but returns in person this year on Thanksgiving morning, November 25. The 20th annual Turkey Trot will be the same 3-mile route on city streets (see attached map). The Trot is a good workout for serious runners, and a benchmark for hundreds of others looking to improve their times from previous races. The race always begins early Thanksgiving morning, – hence its tagline, “Move your feet before you eat!” The Turkey Trot brought in more than 1,200 runners in 2010. The Trot, then in its 9th year, had grown into a large social event. Piedmont residents and neighbors came together walking, jogging, dog-walking, and stroller-pushing. That year also marked a more official race. It was the first year the race used a professional timing service and clock at the finish line. Piedmont Post offered a new award that year for the largest registered family in the trot. The city encouraged runners to “go green,” and observe sustainable practices by supplying water jugs and compostable cups to quench runners’ thirsts. The morning run was followed by refreshments and awards on the high school campus. articles.text: I must take issue with the recent article published in the Post labeled “pouring cold water on net zero pool”. This appears to be a misrepresentation of the comments made by the design team. I believe the gist of the comments was mainly aimed at the reality of issues that the team is aware of and appears to be dedicated to addressing. The article label tends to put the onus on the team, which is unfair and inaccurate. Nevertheless, here are other points to be considered. 1. space for electrification has been an issue for them and those of us advocating all-electric. However, the design has not yet been advanced enough to answer this question; there are still options that need to be considered, e.g., Solar PVT solar tube panels, (smaller size but same capacity as those being considered), and high efficiency heat pumps 2. Other options relate to how EBCE’s contribution could offset needed capacity, and the possibility of off-site solar panels 3. Another salient point raised in the article was “could the city forgo addition design features...” IMO, this has to be seriously considered, it points to the heart of the issue of how much we are willing to sacrifice in favor addressing climate change which, as we all know, the effects of which fall on the futures of these very children that will use the pool. This is a dilemma of needs vs. wants/desires...are we willing to step up to seriously embrace that challenge? Tom Webster is a member of Piedmont Connect.

articles.text: A few weeks ago I wrote that the dictionary is not the arbiter of usage; rather, I made the point that language is dynamic, ever changing, and mirrors societal change. Words suddenly appear, some are tweaked, others all but vanish as we constantly search for ways to give meaning to our experience. Recently I saw an article by Amy Harmon in the New York Times in which she discusses the continuing struggle we have encountered while engaging in a national dialogue about race – the expressions, phrases and the vocabulary. This debate grew especially intense after a long summer of protests in response to the death of George Floyd in 2020. Change was demanded, outrage rippled and surged as streets filled with demonstrators, fists raised as exclamation points, signs and banners held high, putting into words the need for social justice. The assumption was that language, not just spoken but written, could bend culture. From that tumultuous summer came a new lexicon that at times was puzzling and yet still made its way into the public’s consciousness. And so, using Harmon’s wording and my own comments, let me offer some examples. In the recent West Virginia election, conservatives suggested that “Critical Race Theory” was being taught in the public schools. It wasn’t. But perhaps more important, its meaning (with the exception of university seminars) was elusive and its complex definition all but ignored. CRT was also linked to Black Lives Matter, as has the word “microaggression,” another expression that begs for clarification. And there is the placement of an “x” at the end of “Latinx,” a recent appellation that replaces Latino, which is masculine, with a word that is considered gender neutral. Harmon explored the term “implicit bias,” which derived from the work in the 1990s by psychologists, who focused on people who harbored subconscious stereotypes. She noted that “implicit” has recently been replaced with the word “complicit,” an intentional change. And there is, of course, the stand alone word “racism,” which has recently been linked to “systemic” or “structural,” two words that reflect a far broader meaning and imply that racism is not just personal prejudice but extends to laws relating to voting, education, and bank-lending. Harmon also includes in her list the word “BiPoc” (pronounced bye-pock), that can now be found in the new Merriam-Webster Dictionary and widely used on social media. It is meant to demonstrate the severity of racial injustice that is perpetrated against Black and Indigenous people. It does not mean bisexual people of color. Two other words now in use when discussing racial injustice are “equality” and “equity.” The latter has moved into the mainstream, and is meant to convey the embedded disadvantages caused by past and present discrimination. Ultimately, what Harmon is attempting to say in her article is that words do matter. While at times their meaning can be puzzling, even confusing, the goal is still to comment, however imperfectly, on the human condition – such as it is. Chris Honore is a reviewer and longtime columnist in the Post. He may be contact by e-mail at: honore307@gmail.com.
articles.title: The Cartography of Language – Redux

articles.text: Editor: Scouting in Piedmont is a very tight-knit community of people who have all been pursuing scouting for a long time. As such, the scouting community in Piedmont doesn’t experience too much expansion. I believe this is due to a lack of exposure to scouting in general. Scouting is a place where scouts can grow and develop into bright new members of society. Scouting instills life-long valuable lessons that I believe should be stressed upon everyone, whether through school or another source. For scouting to grow into something bigger it is necessary to gain more exposure through media. This brings me to why I am reaching out. I personally think it would be great if scouting can receive more exposure through the Piedmont Post aside from the occasional Eagle Scout newspaper clippings. I love and support what the Piedmont Post is doing for the community of Piedmont and keeping everyone interconnected, and it would be wonderful if scouting was more included in that. articles.text: California is preparing for a winter surge of COVID-19 cases despite a relatively high vaccination percentage among its population, Gov. Gavin Newsom said on November 10. “We have seen some signs that suggest concerns,” Gov. Newsom said during a press briefing. “We have learned over the [last two] years that COVID-19 takes advantage when we put our guard down.” Still, hospitalization rates are much lower this November than one year ago. For example, on November 3, the number of intensive care unit (ICU) patients in the state dropped below 1,000; ICU rates weren’t that low since the end of July. Medical experts warn that, although a large portion of Bay Area residents are vaccinated, those who are most vulnerable and require booster shots are not receiving them. Booster shots are available to all Californians age 18 and older, and are strongly recommended for those over the age of 65. “Waning immunity is real, and boosters do fix waning immunity at least for multiple months, but we are not giving out as many as we need to,” UCSF Epidemiology Professor George Rutherford said. The California Department of Public Health on November 9 announced that local health jurisdictions and providers should proactively outreach to patients who are 65 and older, have underlying medical conditions, or received the Johnson and Johnson COVID vaccine. “In addition, providers should not miss an opportunity to vaccinate the unvaccinated or provide boosters by offering vaccine during routine or non-routine visits to medical offices, clinics, pharmacies, and hospitals,” State Public Health Director Tomas Aragon said. When announcing vaccine availability for children ages 5 to 11, Alameda County Health Officer Dr. Nicolas Moss stressed the importance of inoculation for everyone eligible. “With each new population that becomes eligible for vaccination, we move one step closer to ending the COVID pandemic,” he said. “Now is the time to get yourself and your children vaccinated as we approach winter and the holidays, where we expect to see an increase in cases.” According to the California Department of Public Health, holiday travel and gatherings fueled surges last year, 2020. New case percentages was at its highest in the San Francisco Bay Area the week of December 21, 2020. The state concurrently changed regulations and guidance in the midst of surges to attempt to control the rapid spread of the virus. The color-coded tier system was introduced by Gov. Newsom last year, before Thanksgiving, a major holiday for travel. For those planning to travel for the holidays, the State of California recommends taking a number of precautions. The state advises to keep gatherings small, ensure guests are vaccinated, host parties outdoors when possible, and get tested for COVID-19 prior to and after traveling. A full list of state recommendations can be found at https://covid19.ca.gov/ holidays/. tionnaire on the spot. sites/33953. There is no cost for the test.

articles.text: Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) will welcome the holiday season with the Annual Tree Lighting Ceremony – live – on Wednesday, December 1, at 7:00 p.m. in front of Piedmont Community Hall. The festivities will include caroling by the Troubadours, the high school vocal ensemble, candy canes for guests, and a welcome address from City dignitaries. Children will be greeted by Mrs. Santa Claus and an elf, and the children will talk with Santa outdoors at a safe distance. Special needs children will be able to see Santa at 6:30 p.m. Children can bring letters to Santa and deposit them in a special Santa mailbox with the promise of a reply. A special guest from The Make-A-Wish Foundation/Believe Campaign will light the tree. PBF maintains, installs, and removes the colorful LED lights each year. This also offers community members the opportunity of donating to the Holiday Tree Lighting Fund as a way of extending holiday wishes to their friends and neighbors. Learn more at Piedmont Beautification Foundation website by visiting www.piedmontbeautificationfoundation.org.

pages.text: Wednesday, November 17, 2021 3 COVID UPDATE Experts say COVID surge likely, but less severe than 2020 By Allyson Aleksey California is preparing for a winter surge of COVID-19 cases despite a relatively high vaccination percentage among its population, Gov. Gavin Newsom said on November 10. “We have seen some signs that suggest concerns,” Gov. Newsom said during a press briefing. “We have learned over the [last two] years that COVID-19 takes advantage when we put our guard down.” Still, hospitalization rates are much lower this November than one year ago. For example, on November 3, the number of intensive care unit (ICU) patients in the state dropped below 1,000; ICU rates weren’t that low since the end of July. Medical experts warn that, although a large portion of Bay Area residents are vaccinated, those who are most vulnerable and require booster shots are not receiving them. Booster shots are available to all Californians age 18 and older, and are strongly recommended for those over the age of 65. “Waning immunity is real, and boosters do fix waning immunity at least for multiple months, but we are not giving out as many as we need to,” UCSF Epidemiology Professor George Rutherford said. The California Department of Public Health on November 9 announced that local health jurisdictions and providers should proactively outreach to patients who are 65 and older, have underlying medical conditions, or received the Johnson and Johnson COVID vaccine. “In addition, providers should not miss an opportunity to vaccinate the unvaccinated or provide boosters by offering vaccine during routine or non-routine visits to medical offices, clinics, pharmacies, and hospitals,” State Public Health Director Tomas Aragon said. When announcing vaccine availability for children ages 5 to 11, Alameda County Health Officer Dr. Nicolas Moss stressed the importance of inoculation for everyone eligible. “With each new population that becomes eligible for vaccination, we move one step closer to ending the COVID pandemic,” he said. “Now is the time to get yourself and your children vaccinated as we approach winter and the holidays, where we expect to see an increase in cases.” According to the California Department of Public Health, holiday travel and gatherings fueled surges last year, 2020. New case percentages was at its highest in the San Francisco Bay Area the week of December 21, 2020. The state concurrently changed regulations and guidance in the midst of surges to attempt to control the rapid spread of the virus. The color-coded tier system was introduced by Gov. Newsom last year, before Thanksgiving, a major holiday for travel. For those planning to travel for the holidays, the State of California recommends taking a number of precautions. The state advises to keep gatherings small, ensure guests are vaccinated, host parties outdoors when possible, and get tested for COVID-19 prior to and after traveling. A full list of state recommendations can be found at https://covid19.ca.gov/ holidays/. articles.text: Deadline to apply is December 8 The City of Piedmont is seeking volunteers to serve on the Measure UU Bond Oversight Committee. The deadline to apply is Wednesday, December 8. The committee will consist of five residents who will focus on review and reporting on the expenditure of the proceeds of the bonds. The bonds for the project will be sold on November 18, and interest on the bonds is tax exempt with maturities ranging from 2023 through 2051. The committee will inform the public on how the city is expending the bond proceeds and review expenditure reports produced by the city. Committee members will produce an annual report which will include a statement indicating whether the bonds used are appropriate as set forth in Measure UU, and a summary of the committee’s proceedings and activities for the preceding year. The Bond Oversight Committee is not responsible for managing or directing any pool activities; instead, it will leverage the experience and expertise of its members to ensure bond proceeds are spent in accordance with Ordinance 754 N.S., or Measure UU, passed by voters in November 2020. The committee will meet two times per year throughout the project until the expenditure of the bond proceeds is complete, which is anticipated to be a 24 to 36-month process. Interested residents may download the Application for Appointive Vacancy and/or apply online on the City’s web site at https://piedmont.ca.gov. Applications are due to City Hall by Wednesday, December 8 at 5:00 p.m. Interviews with the City Council for these positions will be scheduled for the evening of Monday, December 13, 2021. No appointments will be made without a Council interview. Residents with questions are invited to contact the City Clerk’s office at (510) 420-3040. articles.text: Laura Pochop As Laura and I enter our family’s final year in the Piedmont schools, our contribution to The Giving Campaign means more to us than ever. Not just a donation, but a huge thank you to our schools and the teachers for everything they have given to our family. This year when we wrote our check to The Giving Campaign, we felt an overwhelming sense of gratitude and a tremendous appreciation for all that the Piedmont schools have done for our three kids. We have a few precious months left in the schools. Our son Charlie is a senior and he is almost to the finish line. This is a bittersweet time for sure. Eighteen years have passed since our first, Tess, entered Ms. Sandy’s kindergarten class in the fall of 2003. It brings tears to our eyes to think of those first days at drop off when we met the other new parents on the Havens playground. Those “new” parents are now our life-long friends; those kindergartners are now adults; and Havens looks like a Four Seasons Hotel. The incredible things our schools and teachers have given our kids are too numerous to count and difficult to put into words. Put simply, our children are good people. They are kind and thoughtful. No doubt our kids are going to thrive and we’re incredibly proud of them. We credit their teachers and the Piedmont schools, and we are profoundly grateful. We hope the parents of seniors, and particularly those like us who are months away from being empty nesters, will consider a donation to The Giving Campaign. This year, more than any other, it feels like the right thing to do. of heart and spirit.

Today it’s odd to reflect about how remote the location was to Paris-proper, but even at the end of the 18th century this area east Marquetry floor, antechamber to dining room. Its age is 250 years. Les Cabinet des Glaces (mirrors) of the Tuileries was still hinterland. The twin limestone palais were built at a countryside setting so rough the site bordered on a drainage ditch, and the exterior grounds were without electric lighting except for a floodlight mount on each building. These factors mattered two decades later when revolution broke out and the royal warehouse was looted. The crown assigned the Royal Garde-Meuble to maintain and protect the furniture as early as 1764. But, as the nation fell into chaos and the king’s grasp on power slipped away, the deux palais on a country road were not well-guarded. One commander reported that he needed 60 guards and he had only 12. It was common knowledge that the inventory at the keep was not just limited to the royal furniture: the keep contained the royal collection of diamonds. An extraordinar y theft occurred in September 1792 at the height of political intrigue and chaos for Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette who were by then under prison guard after the Flight to Varennes, a foiled attempt to flee east by coaches to Germany and assemble a foreign army to crush the revolutionaries. Thieves freely entered the Garde-Meuble spending five days digging out their bounty and stealing the crown’s collection of massively large diamonds. Some gems were recovered, but not the 68-carat Blue Diamond believed to have been carried to England where it was professionally cut to camouflage the massive stone. The 45-carat Hope Diamond on display at the Smithsonian, the French claim, is the French Blue. articles.text: Piedmont’s water polo team, seeded No. 3, lost to No. 2 Marin Academy in the North Coast Section semifinals 7-4 at Redwood HS in Larkspur on Wednesday, November 10. It was their first semifinals appearance since 2018 after reaching the quarterfinals in 2019 prior to the pandemic. The team finished a successful season with a 19-6 record. It was a defensive battle from the get-go. The Highlanders led 3-2 with less than a minute before halftime, but Marin tied it with 11 seconds to spare. From there, the Wildcats’ defense prevented clean shooting lanes. Brit Burden had two goals for Piedmont in the NCS Semifinals. “We got tired in the second half. Our offense lost steam, but our defense was fine. If we only give up seven [goals], that’s a score we can live with. We played a long season; our boys got tired and have been sick. We played in this big pool, [Marin Academy] had the endurance and we didn’t,” said PHS coach John Savage. Piedmont typically plays in a 25-yard pool, while Redwood’s pool is an official 25-meter length. Senior leader Antonio Rivera compared this match to the WACC Championship win at Encinal in Alameda. “Compared to the Encinal pool, you can tell it’s a lot bigger which means a lot more swimming. It racks up. The meters take a toll on your body; you get tired in the second half, But it’s all about persevering through it. Playing in a larger pool gives you more space offensively but it’s also more tiring because it spreads you out more,” said Rivera. The appeal of goalie Dariush Kashani’s suspension was successful after the NCS ruled that the goalie’s involvement in a fracas during a match with Terra Linda was erroneous. This meant the Highlanders could lean on its defense, once again, and force shots from the perimeter. Returning to the team next year will be Kashani along with strong-arm scoring sophomore Peter Krumins, and starters George Stein and Britt Burden. “We had a lot of seniors when I was a freshman and we learned from them. This year we learned from the seniors again. We just filled in, saw the role we had to play and played that role. Not many people expected us to go this far or win league. It was a really great season,” said Krumins. Game Recap The Highlanders ended the first quarter trailing 1-0, but led 3-2 in the seconds prior to halftime before Marin tied it at 3-3. The Wildcats stormed ahead in the third quarter with two goals, and closed out the game at 7-4. Piedmont was able to kill en exclusion penalty in the first minute of action, but went down at the 4:07 mark by Marin Academy’s Schuyler Rewick. In the second quarter, Rivera tied the game in the early minutes at 5:23 and the Highlanders went up ahead on Rivera’s second goal with 3:25 after they drew a man-advantage. But their joy was short-lived when MA’s Connor Dickinson scored just 12 seconds later. With 1:05 left, PHS went up 3-2 on a goal by Burden, but the Wildcats’ 2 scored again at 11 seconds, 3-3, at the half. Staff Photos Antonio Rivera scored two goals against Marin Academy. articles.text: Playing at home and seeded No. 4 in the post-season, Piedmont’s tennis team was upended by No 5 College Prep in the quarterfinals of the North Coast Section Team Championship on Thursday, November 11. One day earlier Piedmont defeated No 13 Justin Siena in Napa, 5-2, in the first round of NCS play. “It was a tough match, but that’s the way things go sometimes,” said coach Jim Landes. “We started strong and swept doubles, but College Prep’s singles did well to close out their matches. They were all really close.” CPS beat Piedmont by winning three of the four singles matches in three sets. Piedmont finished its season with an overall record of 18-9. Piedmont has enjoyed years of success in the North Coast Section team championship. It won the first year the tournament was created, in 1998, and has since won 11 titles. Its most recent NCS title was in 2018, and it was ranked No. 1 in 2019 when smoke from wildfires caused delays and the eventual cancellation of the 2019 tournament. Game Recap The day started well against CPS with Piedmont leading 3-1 after sweeping all three doubles matches. However Prep swept all four singles matches to claim the upset. In doubles, sophomore Cecilia Defazio and freshman Emma Eisemon cruised to a straight set 7-5, 6-0 win at No. 3 spot. It was a dominant season for the two young doubles starters, winning 10 matches this season. “They play really well together and had a really great season. They earned a starting spot on varsity and proved they belong here. That’s tough to do as a freshman or sophomore,” said Landes. Junior Mara LaForte and senior Audrey Frankel than won 6-2, 6-4 at No. 2 doubles, and soon after No. 1 doubles Amanda Becker and Audrey Mahany also won in straight sets, 6-0, 7-5. articles.text: Judy Chicago’s On Fire at 80 is on display at the DeYoung Museum. A retrospective art exhibit celebrating the pioneering feminist artist Judy Chicago is now on display at the de Young museum in San Francisco, continuing through January 9. Chicago is one of the founding figures behind the 1970’s feminist art movement. Her storied career is highlighted through her colorful works on canvas, porcelain plates, car hoods and more. The exhibition will include approximately 130 paintings, prints, drawings and sculptures by the artist. The exhibit was curated in conjunction with the 100th anniversary of women’s right to vote in the United States, and pays homage to Chicago who fought against the suppression of women’s creativity. She founded the first feminist arts education program in the country at California State University in Fresno. To purchase tickets to the exhibition, visit https://deyoung. famsf.org/exhibitions/judy-chicago.

articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD), a Smithsonian affiliate, presents an exhibition in partnership with Contemporary Arts Museum Houston entitled “Amoako Boafo: Soul of Black Folks.” The exhibition will be on display through February 27. The show is a solo exhibition by Ghanian artist Amoako Boafo, who is displaying more than 20 works created between 2018 and 2021. Curated by Larry Ossei-Mensah, it displays the artists’ paintings that actively center Black subjectivity anchored by his extremely calculated brushwork and finger-painted strokes. Boafo’s paintings are intimately connected to his experience as a Ghanaian artist living and working between Vienna, Austria, and Accra, Ghana. articles.text: In a special chamber music concert offered by Berkeley Symphony, legendary violinist Stuart Canin will perform at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Sunday afternoon, November 21, at 4 p.m. Titled Stuart Canin & Friends, he will be accompanied by Helen Wickett on piano, and joined by Berkeley Symphony Artistic Director Rene Mandel. The program includes Five Pieces for Two Violins and Piano by Shostokovich, Stravinsky’s Divertimento for Violin and Piano, and Beethoven’s Sonata for Violin and Piano in C Minor. Tickets are available through Berkeley Symphony by calling the Symphony Box Office at (510) 841-2800, ext. 1, or online at https://tickets.berkeleysymphony.org/TheatreManager/1/ online?performance=532. Stuart Canin, Violin Stuart Canin was born in New York City and studied the violin with famed pedagogues Hans Letz and Ivan Galmanian. As a young violinist Canin received nationwide attention at age 10 when he appeared on the Fred Allen radio show and performed Schubert’s The Bee, helping start the famous radio feud between Allen and Jack Benny. During World War II Canin was sent lo Europe as an infantryman. When the war ended he was sent to Paris to help entertain Allied troops. In July 1945 he and pianist Eugene List were called to Potsdam, Germany for a private concert for U.S. President Harry Truman, English Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Russian Premier Josef Stalin. The event was reported throughout the world. He returned to the U.S in 1946 and continued his music education. In 1953 he was appointed music professor at Iowa State. In 1956 he was a Fulbright professor at the Hochschule in Freiburg, Germany. Three years later, in 1959, he won the International Paganini Violin Competition in Genoa, Italy, selected over 24 other violinists. He was the first American to win the prize. He joined the faculty at Oberlin Conservatory of Music in 1961 as a professor, and left in 1966 to accept a position as Concertmaster of the Chamber Symphony of Philadelphia. In 1970 Seiji Ozawa appointed him Concertmaster of the San Francisco Symphony, where he remained for 10 years. Starting in 1980, he worked on music scores for Hollywood films, eventually working in more than 650 films. He returned to San Francisco in 1992 and founded the New Century Chamber Orchestra. Helene Wickett, Piano Hélène Wickett has appeared as piano soloist with major orchestras and in solo recitals throughout Europe and America. Her orchestral appearances include 70 different concertos with major orchestras, including San Francisco Symphony, Boston Symphony, Cleveland Orchestra, Dallas Symphony, at the BBC in London and orchestras in France, Austria, Holland, Ireland, Sweden, Spain, Norway and Denmark, Poland, and the Czech Republic. She has played solo programs in virtually every western musical capital, including acclaimed recitals at London’s Wigmore Hall, Paris’ Opéra Comique, Salle Gaveau and Salle Cortot, Rome’s Villa Medici, Washington’s Kennedy Center and New York’s Carnegie Hall. She studied with Alfred Brendel, Nadia Boulanger, Robert Casadesus, Geneviève Joy, Elena Guirola Hitchcock, and Benjamin Kaplan. The winner of the Pro Musici’s Foundation Competition, she has had works dedicated to her by Darius Milhaud, Andrew Imbrie, Robert Rodriguez and Hsueh-Yung Shen. She also performs as an orchestral violinist and violist, having studied with Stuart Canin, Henryk Szeryng and Jacob Krachmalnick. Fluent in half a dozen languages, she works with singers and assists opera productions from the keyboard and as supertitle operator. She currently teaches privately in San Mateo. Rene’ Mandel, Violin Rene Mandel enjoys a night off from his role as Executive Director of Berkeley Symphony and a rare opportunity to perform as violinist. A Los Angeles native, he began playing the violin the Violinist Stuart Canin age of 8. At 14, he performed as soloist with the Los Angeles Philharmonic, conducted by Calvin Simmons. At 20, he became a member of the Los Angeles Chamber Orchestra and became Principal 2nd violin. In 1993 he was a founding member of the New Century Chamber Orchestra under Stuart Canin. He has performed as soloist with the San Francisco Ballet Orchestra, the New Century Chamber Orchestra, and the Knoxville Symphony. As an orchestral violinist, he has performed and toured with the San Francisco Symphony and the Los Angeles Philharmonic. As a chamber musician, he has performed throughout the United States and Europe. His teachers included Mr. Canin at UC Santa Barbara, where he earned his Bachelor of Music degree. In 2006 he served as Orchestra Manager and Artistic Administrator for Berkeley Symphony under the direction of Kent Nagano. From 2009-2011 he was Director of Artistic Operations/Executive Producer for the Orchestre Symphonique de Montréal, again under Kent Nagano. He returned to the Bay Area in July 2011 as Executive Director for Berkeley Symphony, under the direction of Joana Carneiro. articles.text: With a resplendent silvery half-moon radiating over the City, you knew this would be a very special concert. Apprehension had been palpable as the recently retired music director Michael Tilson Thomas, turning 77 next month, underwent brain surgery to remove a tumor. Forced to cancel guest engagements with four orchestras, he made it back November 12-13 despite all adversity. He was a mite shaky, a mite cautious, but as confident and verbose as ever conducting the San Francisco Symphony. The instant he came on stage a rousing shout and a standing ovation by the audience brought things to a standstill, coming from a crowd fervently wishing for his total recuperation. Clearly, he is and was esteemed and beloved. His program was a careful one, devoid of unfamiliar music or technical knots. The highlight was the 15-minute Notturno (Nocturne) from 2004 composed by the conductor himself – a flight of fancy for solo flute (Demarre McGill) and string orchestra. The stamp of Italy was on the score, which even quoted discreetly from the Sextet of Donizetti’s opera Lucia di Lammermoor in the strings’ pizzicato. On hearing it, you might mistake this for a 19th century work – modernisms were studiously avoided in order to plumb a specific milieu. Demarre is a stellar new name on the scene, though not McGill; his brother, the renowned clarinetist Anthony, has played the area repeatedly. Demarre, currently with the Seattle Symphony, would make a terrific match as principal with Michael Tilson Thomas returned to conduct the San Francisco Symphony on November 12 and 13. the SFS, which now has a yawning vacancy, particularly if he ever could stay still. Performing MTT’s piece, he was restless and wide-ranging, adding a visual element to the auditory. Demarre could fill a double void in the SFS, which like many professional orchestras around the country has no Black personnel playing on stage regularly. He played the fast-flying and bird-call effects to the hilt, as trilling as they were thrilling. He produced a sensual flow in the many lyrical sections and brought off quasi-improvisatory sections delectably. The SFS’s string orchestra fell in behind him, as if long-time collaborators. In his flawless impromptu introduction to the piece, MTT spoke of the work as an existential quest, with the flutist pondering, what am I doing here? McGill, I thought, answered that query several times over with his committed playing. The concert had as bookends Mozart’s Six German Dances, which Mozart had dashed off in record time over a single brief sitting, and the first (Spring) of the Schumann Symphonies, which to these ears have always resonated as a quasi-Prussian opus of unwavering severity – perhaps springtime at a boot camp. MUSIC NOTES MTT’s successor, Esa-Pekka Salonen, has his work cut out for him, not only conducting regularly, but also working to help fill at least 11 vacancies on the SFS roster, including the #1 and #2 members of the flute section. In addition, there are slots open in the cello section (including the principal), two more in the clarinets, and assorted openings in violin, viola, bassoon, trombone and percussion. MTT is returning to the podium in measured steps. For Nov. 18-20, he is conducting only Copland’s Appalachian Spring, which he has led many times. The rest of the program will feature Ludovic Morot on the podium.

articles.text: A scene from Stuart Little. Stuart Little is a live action/ animated family friendly feature, based on the 1945 best-selling novel by E.B. White. Kids, for generations, have been enamored with this small anthropogenic mouse, and will find much to enjoy in this adaptation. The story begins when Mr. and Mrs. Little (Hugh Laurie and Geena Davis) visit an orphanage where they meet and decide to adopt Stuart (Michael J. Fox). When they bring him home, he is not greeted all that warmly by the older son, George Little (Jonathan Lipki), who resents having a new brother. And there’s the family cat, Snowball (Nathan Lane) who takes one look at Stuart and views him as dinner. And so, things don’t get off to a good start for Stuart. George unintentionally throws him down the laundry chute along with the laundry. Mrs. Little manages to put him in the washing machine where Stuart swallows a mouthful of detergent. Before long Stuart begins to feel lonely and a bit of an outcast from the family. As a result, the Littles return to the orphanage and speak with its owner, Mrs. Keeper (Julia Sweeney), asking if it would be possible to find Stuart’s biological parents. And thus begins Stuart’s adventure. He does end up bonding with George when he helps him win a remote-controlled sailboat race. Meanwhile Snowball’s alley cat friend, Monty (Steve Zahn), visits the Littles’ home and discovers that Stuart is a new addition to the family. Snowball and Monty report Stuart’s presence to the leader of the alley cat cohort, Smokey (Chazz Palminteri), who devises a nasty plan for Stuart. The Littles learn from Mrs. Keeper that Mr. and Mrs. Stout (Bruno Kirby and Jennifer Tilly) arrived at the orphanage, claiming to be Stuart’s real parents (they’re in collusion with Smokey) and they have left with Stuart. But the Littles soon learn from Mrs. Keeper that Stuart’s parents died years before in an accident, and that the Stouts are imposters. The Littles, upset, call the police, who begin the search for Stuart, whose life they fear is in danger. There are exciting moments, tense chases through Central Park, and lots more going on, to include a rescue of Snowball by, as it turns out, Stuart. Ultimately, Snowball and Stuart return home, and the Little family is happily reunited. Kids will love the excitement, and the animation/live action is seamless and wonderfully done. Stuart Little. Live action and animated family comedy. Directed by Rob Minkoff. Starring Geena Davis, Hugh Laurie, and the voice of Michael J. Fox. 1 hr., 32 min. Rated PG.

articles.text: Howard Ratner (Adam Sandler), a New York jeweler, is a man riffing through life – manic, frenetic, impulsively self-destructive, a catastrophe of bad decision-making. From the opening scenes of Uncut Gems Howard is like a frog in a simmering pot of water and it’s he who is turning up the flame. It’s clear from the fraught get-go that this character study will not end well. The only question asked of the audience is how much sustained, fevered frenzy can be endured as Sandler delivers one of his best dramatic performances. A compulsive gambler, he rushes along the gritty streets of New York, engaging in the briefest of conversations, pausing just long enough to make (or promises to make) a deal, or come up with some overdue cash. His hustle is perpetual, his reedy, grating voice pitched just close enough to panic to sound like fingernails on a chalk board. There’s no moment in Uncut Gems of expository relief. His life is frantically dodgy, bowling pins thrown in the air. He seems perpetually oblivious to the fact that his shtick grows increasingly frayed: he’s in hock to some thugs, one being his brother-inlaw (Eric Bogosian), for serious money. He’s also obsessing about a South African rock embedded with uncut stones that he’s going to take to auction, convinced it is worth some $300,000. While the rock is the story’s McGuffin, it’s also a detour, as events ricochet through his life. He actually lets a famous basketball star (Kevin Garnett playing himself) take the rock with him for the night, leaving as collateral his Celtic championship ring, which Howard promises to hold until the next day when the rock is returned. He, of course, sells the ring and bets the cash on a Celtics game. Meanwhile, Howard is juggling an angry wife (Idina Menzel), a young mistress (Julia Fox), and argues with both, loudly (loud is his default setting), all while conducting his life like a Adam Sandler stars in Uncut Gems. pyramid scheme. The anxiety (for the audience) is relentless as he pinballs from side to side in search of a flipper, kvetching and promising and careening toward a climax that is breathtaking and takes place inside his hot house gem shop. This long scene is focused on the outcome of that Celtics game. Howard paces and yells as baskets are missed or made. The thugs, there to collect money owed, throw him malevolent looks while sitting on the other side of a shatterproof glass security wall. This is the same outfit that stripped Howard naked, threw him into the back of his SUV, wanting to impress upon him that they take his debt seriously. Some final thoughts about Uncut Gems: Sandler is extraordinary in his portrayal of Howard Ratner. He mines every quirk, every irrational moment. He inhabits the character, giving depth to a man who engages when he should retreat, seeks confrontation when he should walk away, agrees when he should disagree, is obnoxious when diplomacy is called for. He’s a mess, yet remains optimistic, a driven gamer who thrives on chaos. It’s impossible not to watch Sandler chew up the scenery. For sibling directors Josh and Benny Safdie it’s clear that Howard is the quintessential uncut gem. Uncut Gems. Directed by Ben and Joshua Safdie. Starring Adam Sandler, Julia Fox, Lekeith Standfield. 2 hrs., 15 min. Rated R.

articles.text: Dane DeHaan, Christoph Waltz and Alicia Vikander star in Tulip Fever. The year is 1634. The place is Amsterdam, a thriving port city defined by international shipping, art patronage and likely the first western commodities bubble: a frenetic speculation in tulip bulbs, most especially a bulb referred to as “the breaker.” In the backrooms of taverns, buyers and sellers carried on the purchase and sale of bulbs with all the enthusiasm of traders on the floor of the Chicago Mercantile Exchange. Most coveted was the white tulip – the breaker – that had a glorious streak of crimson on one petal. It sold for stunning prices, hence the title of the film, Tulip Fever. But this is not simply a story about the fortunes made and lost in tulip speculation (to include occasional suicides in one of the many canals). Indeed, while the operative word is “fever,” it also applies to an adulterous triangle between a young woman, Sophia (Alicia Vikander), who was all but purchased from a local orphanage by a wealthy merchant, Cornelis (Christoph Waltz), a sixty-something man. Having lost his first wife and child in childbirth, he is now looking for a vessel to carry an heir. Sophia, lovely, grateful to suddenly find herself surrounded by affluence, does what she can to encourage the hopes of impregnation. However, after three years, and no success, Cornelis considers returning Sophia to the orphanage. In the interim, he decides to immortalize himself and Sophia in a painting and hires a young artist, Jan van Loos (Dane DeHann), to create a formally posed portrait. And so enters into the home a young, vital, attractive painter who cannot take his eyes off of Sophia whose luminous visage is reflected in the light of the morning sun as she stands near a window holding a breaker tulip. Hence, while tulip fever grips Amsterdam, a different fever grips Sophia and Jan It is immediately clear that their carnal attraction will likely end badly. How the last half of act two and act three crystalize involves a convoluted plan that requires a certain suspension of disbelief. Perhaps it’s a cliché that the husband is the last to know. When he learns of the ninemonth charade that has been swirling around him he is flummoxed. Involved in this drama is the Abbess of the orphanage (Judi Dench), an ethically challenged, lecherous doctor, a type of surrogate pregnancy involving Sophia’s housemaid, Maria (Halliday Granger), and an obscure but interesting ending. Did I like the story? I did. It is lushly told, beautifully costumed, with a consummately gifted cast, beginning with three Oscar winners: Dench, Vikander and Waltz. Tulip Fever. Directed by Justin Chadwick. Starring Alicia Vikander, Dane DeHaan, Christoph Waltz. 1 hr., 47 min. Rated R.

articles.text: Former Piedmont resident Lisa Riddiough’s first novel, Elvis and the World as it Stands, published in August, is now available for purchase online and in select stores. Riddiough’s debut novel is appropriate for students age 10 and up and is a narrative of loss and chosen families, told from the point of view of a newly-adopted kitten named Elvis. Riddiough said she drew the story from her own experience as a volunteer for East Bay SPCA, and decided upon the unorthodox approach of using an animal as the protagonist and narrator. In the book, Elvis is adopted by the Pemberton family, but in the process is separated from his sister, Etta. Elvis’ mission is to be reunited with Etta. “I volunteered with the East Bay SPCA’s feline department with my daughter Julia, and there were many kittens over that period that were adopted out to their forever homes, but in the process were separated from [siblings] they had bonded to,” she said. “I wanted to explore that feeling of not having control over what happens to you.” Riddiough mirrored the feelings of hopelessness Elvis the cat felt to his human companion and deuteragonist Georgina Pemberton, a 10-year-old girl who is navigating the grief of her parent’s separation. The book balances these heavy themes of divorce and loss with the light-hearted animal characters that become Elvis’ friends Book jacket of Elvis and the World as it Stands. Author Lisa Riddiough and confidants, which includes an overly-optimistic hamster and an inquisitive goldfish. “I have an ensemble cast of animal characters that live in the home Elvis is adopted into. I tried to bring in humor to balance the heavier topics,” Riddiough explained. Georgina’s affinity for Lego toys and building well-known skyscrapers with them allows the book to touch lightly on 9/11, extending the theme of “a loss of control.” The title Elvis and the World as it Stands makes reference to the kitten who is beginning to make sense of the world around him. “The events surrounding that day (Sept. 11) made a lot of adults around the world feel a sense of losing control,” Riddiough said. “But the important [message in the novel] is, how do we move forward? For Elvis and Georgina, it is with the support of friends and family, and a strong sense of purpose.” Riddiough began taking writing classes in her mid-forties through the University of California extension. When writing her first book, she said she was “amazed” at how much she learned through the publishing process and working with an agent. The story sold at the beginning of the COVID lockdown and was published in August this year. Riddiough’s next book, Letters to Live By: an alphabet book with intention, will be released in January 2022. The book is dedicated to a Piedmont middle school teacher who Riddiough said her children greatly admired. Lisa Riddiough’s novel Elvis and the World as it Stands now available By Allyson Aleksey Former Piedmont resident Lisa Riddiough’s first novel, Elvis and the World as it Stands, published in August, is now available for purchase online and in select stores. Riddiough’s debut novel is appropriate for students age 10 and up and is a narrative of loss and chosen families, told from the point of view of a newly-adopted kitten named Elvis. Riddiough said she drew the story from her own experience as a volunteer for East Bay SPCA, and decided upon the unorthodox approach of using an animal as the protagonist and narrator. In the book, Elvis is adopted by the Pemberton family, but in the process is separated from his sister, Etta. Elvis’ mission is to be reunited with Etta. “I volunteered with the East Bay SPCA’s feline department with my daughter Julia, and there were many kittens over that period that were adopted out to their forever homes, but in the process were separated from [siblings] they had bonded to,” she said. “I wanted to explore that feeling of not having control over what happens to you.” Riddiough mirrored the feelings of hopelessness Elvis the cat felt to his human companion and deuteragonist Georgina Pemberton, a 10-year-old girl who is navigating the grief of her parent’s separation. The book balances these heavy themes of divorce and loss with the light-hearted animal characters that become Elvis’ friends Book jacket of Elvis and the World as it Stands. Author Lisa Riddiough and confidants, which includes an overly-optimistic hamster and an inquisitive goldfish. “I have an ensemble cast of animal characters that live in the home Elvis is adopted into. I tried to bring in humor to balance the heavier topics,” Riddiough explained. Georgina’s affinity for Lego toys and building well-known skyscrapers with them allows the book to touch lightly on 9/11, extending the theme of “a loss of control.” The title Elvis and the World as it Stands makes reference to the kitten who is beginning to make sense of the world around him. “The events surrounding that day (Sept. 11) made a lot of adults around the world feel a sense of losing control,” Riddiough said. “But the important [message in the novel] is, how do we move forward? For Elvis and Georgina, it is with the support of friends and family, and a strong sense of purpose.” Riddiough began taking writing classes in her mid-forties through the University of California extension. When writing her first book, she said she was “amazed” at how much she learned through the publishing process and working with an agent. The story sold at the beginning of the COVID lockdown and was published in August this year. Riddiough’s next book, Letters to Live By: an alphabet book with intention, will be released in January 2022. The book is dedicated to a Piedmont middle school teacher who Riddiough said her children greatly admired. articles.text: The rain had come and gone, and Wednesday, November 10, was a beautiful day for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group to explore more Piedmont streets. Another strong turnout of 25 walkers arrived at the Exedra: Sherry Jacobs, Noemi Alvarado, Mike Henn, Melba Yee, Pat Keller, Siow Fang Tan, Emma Sangil, Charlene Louie, Monica Calliste, Dena Belinkoff, Jim Kellogg, Priscilla Wanerus, Alicia Rivera, Ken Young, Nancy Henn, Elangovan Shanmuga Sundaram, Pat McMahon, Lois Price, Hellen Dong, Quincy Dong, Stella Houston, Alan Goldhammer, Carole Lyons, Wenny Young, Tami DeSellier, Jim Kuo, and Dick Carter. The group was joined by Jill and Ron Day from England who were making a long-delayed visit with their son, daughter-in-law, and two granddaughters in Piedmont. The chosen location last week was Rose Avenue and Nace Avenue and nearby streets on the southwest edge of Piedmont at the Oakland border. This part of Piedmont goes back to the city’s early days, shortly after its founding in 1907. Nace, Howard, and Lake were are built around 1908. The oldest houses on Nace are the “Gibson House” (46 Nace), built in 1910, and the “Govan House” (18 Nace) built in 1911. Pat Keller, a walker, said her home on Nace was built in 1914. The walkers crossed Oakland Avenue to Latham Street, Piedmont’s only street named Street. Most others are Avenue or Road or Drive. Continuing on Greenbank Avenue they arrived at Rose Avenue, where they admired the beautiful, old, gingerbread Victorian homes, one with a rooster weathervane. The homes are beautifully maintained, colorful, and rival those in San Francisco. At the end of Rose they came to Kingston Avenue, and then past Beach School on Lake, and then up to Nace, one of the city’s L-shaped streets. As luck would have it, David Yam was coming out of his house, the “Gibson house’ on Nace. Warren Gibson, whose family had lived in the house it for 70 years, was a woodworking teacher at Oakland Tech and had done incredible detail work inside the house. The catalpa tree the Gibsons planted in the 1920s, nearly 100 years ago, is now huge. The walkers returned via Cambridge Way, which has two large palm trees, then up Greenbank to San Carlos and Magnolia. When the walkers arrived at the Exedra they invited their new English friends, the Days, to join future Wednesday walks while they are in town. The day was a four-mile exploration with new and old friends, and some unexpected Piedmont history. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. 3820 Broadway, Oakland Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03

articles.text: Mitch Winters sister Elizabeth As a Troop 15 leader has written about Mitch, “he was a significant role model for many scouts.” Mitch was also part of the Piedmont Police Department’s Police Explorer’s Program, devoting approximately 350 hours/year to it. He helped with crowd and traffic safety at beloved town events like the Fourth of July parade and the Fallfest 5K run. Ultimately Mitch’s peers selected him as the Sergeant of the Explorers program. And he was part of the Piedmont Explorer team that went to the 2015 SWAT Tactical Competition in Chandler, AZ and, in a series of David-v.-Goliath-type upsets, placed first in 3 out of 11 events against better-funded teams from much bigger cities. This trip was when Mitch first started to fall in love with Arizona. With his parents’ permission, while still in high school, Mitch committed to the United States Marine Corps as an Infantryman. Mitch turned down admission to The Citadel because he wanted to start serving this country right away. He left for basic training two days after graduating from high school. In the Corps, he was deployed overseas for eight months, earned a meritorious promotion, won a National Defense Medal, was an Infantry Squad Leader, a Combat Marksmanship Coach, and a graduate of the brutal Marine Corps Water Survival School. In his off hours, he became a cross-fit enthusiast and a Brazilian Jiu Jitsu devotee—and he won his second tournament. He was honorably discharged from the Corps after four years of service. In June of this year, he graduated from the Mesa Arizona Policy Academy, full of joy, hope, and optimism—his natural state. He was so looking forward to being, as he put it, “out on the street.” As Phase 1 of a four-phase field training program, he was assigned to “Central Graves”—Central Mesa, the graveyard shift. Mesa is afflicted by the high crime rates that its two principal national gangs, MS-13 and the Aryan Brotherhood, inflict on it. Mitch was assigned a Field Training Officer (“FTO”) nicknamed “The Hunter”— someone who would proactively look for gang activity and get those gang members off the street. Mitch loved it. pages.text: Wednesday, November 17, 2021 25 Mitchell William Winters, raised in Piedmont and a graduate of the Piedmont schools, died on Friday, November 12, 2021, at the age of 23. He leaves behind a legacy of which anyone, of any age, would be justifiably proud. From the age of 8, all he ever wanted to do was serve this country, first in the United States Marine Corps and then as a police officer. He achieved both of those dreams—after starting early in his life to work towards them. While attending the Piedmont Schools, he developed a deep love for the Boy Scouts of America’s youth programs of character development and values-based leadership training. A member of Piedmont’s vaunted Troop 15, Mitch achieved various leadership positions, including as the Troop Representative to the Order of the Arrow. He also graduated from the Boy Scouts of America’s National Youth Leadership Training program and thereafter served on the Staff and as a Team Guide for that program. Ultimately, he earned the rank of Eagle Scout. His Eagle Scout project was informed and inspired by contact with the Oakland Police Department’s K-9 training facility; Mitch had seen the training officers eating lunch without a place to sit. So he built and installed a picnic table and benches for them. Mitch Winters Celebrating the great outdoors. Mitch and his sister Elizabeth In Memoriam Mitchell William Winters As a Troop 15 leader has written about Mitch, “he was a significant role model for many scouts.” Mitch was also part of the Piedmont Police Department’s Police Explorer’s Program, devoting approximately 350 hours/year to it. He helped with crowd and traffic safety at beloved town events like the Fourth of July parade and the Fallfest 5K run. Ultimately Mitch’s peers selected him as the Sergeant of the Explorers program. And he was part of the Piedmont Explorer team that went to the 2015 SWAT Tactical Competition in Chandler, AZ and, in a series of David-v.-Goliath-type upsets, placed first in 3 out of 11 events against better-funded teams from much bigger cities. This trip was when Mitch first started to fall in love with Arizona. With his parents’ permission, while still in high school, Mitch committed to the United States Marine Corps as an Infantryman. Mitch turned down admission to The Citadel because he wanted to start serving this country right away. He left for basic training two days after graduating from high school. In the Corps, he was deployed overseas for eight months, earned a meritorious promotion, won a National Defense Medal, was an Infantry Squad Leader, a Combat Marksmanship Coach, and a graduate of the brutal Marine Corps Water Survival School. In his off hours, he became a cross-fit enthusiast and a Brazilian Jiu Jitsu devotee—and he won his second tournament. He was honorably discharged from the Corps after four years of service. In June of this year, he graduated from the Mesa Arizona Policy Academy, full of joy, hope, and optimism—his natural state. He was so looking forward to being, as he put it, “out on the street.” As Phase 1 of a four-phase field training program, he was assigned to “Central Graves”—Central Mesa, the graveyard shift. Mesa is afflicted by the high crime rates that its two principal national gangs, MS-13 and the Aryan Brotherhood, inflict on it. Mitch was assigned a Field Training Officer (“FTO”) nicknamed “The Hunter”— someone who would proactively look for gang activity and get those gang members off the street. Mitch loved it. He thrived on it. He called us each week, in calls that would last an hour or more, to regale us with stories of the arrests that he had helped and the events on his shift. He loved Central Graves, and he admired and respected The Hunter. He could not wait to finish his field training program so that he could get “out on the street.” Something happened in Phase 2. On Friday, November 12, 2021—a date his family will never be able to forget, a date that will always be twenty-four hours of the blackest night—Mitch walked into his apartment bedroom, lay down on his bed, and shot himself. We had always known that Mitch had the ability to touch many different people in many different spheres of life. It’s only through his death that we have seen how true that was. We have had everyone from the son of a janitor to former United States Ambassadors reach out to tell us how much they admired Mitch and how sorry they are for our, their, and the country’s loss. And his (it turns out, quite extended) Marine family is bereft. Dozens of his former Marine buddies (a term Marines use to apply both to men and women) have reached out to us to convey their sorrow and share in our grief. To a person, they have told us that they loved Mitch. That he was a “great man”— although, being Marines, they salt up the language with words that a family newspaper can’t print. That he was a “natural leader” who “trained us well” and who “made us want to stand a little taller and straighter.” That, although it wasn’t his job to do so, Mitch was always making time to help his fellow Marines with their troubles and struggles, whether those were large or small. When I finally reached the Staff Sergeant who recruited Mitch into the Corps, and told him the news, the line went Mitch Winters by a Piedmont Police Department patrol car. silent for about 15 seconds. And then was filled with sobbing for about the next three minutes. He kept saying “I’m sorry, sir” (Marines call male civilians “sir”) but couldn’t contain the wellspring of grief that sprung from his core. He loved my son. He introduced my son to the Corps, which helped to turn Mitch into the very fine man that he was. I will always be in the Staff Sergeant’s debt. But in this call, I ended up consoling him. Our family will be hosting a memorial for Mitch at the Claremont Country Club on December 5th, in the afternoon and early evening. The Club was important to Mitch. Its Head of Security, legendary ex-Oakland gang and drug police officer John Gutierrez, gave Mitch his first law-enforcement-type job there as a Security Guard. If you knew Mitch and want to honor his memory, please come. (The Club has a dress code that, in the past, it has always enforced, so perhaps best to call ahead about it.) Dear friends of ours have set up a caring bridge, if you are so inclined, at https://www. caringbridge.org/public/mitchellwinters. Finally, and most important, if you are, or someone you know is, struggling with thoughts of suicide, reach out to someone for help. Mitch has been uniformly and widely described to us as the last person anyone thought would kill himself. We thought that, too; his last words to us, the night before he died, were “I love you.” We love you, too, Mitch. As I’ve said to you and your sister since you were little, I love you like the stars above. By Vernon M. Winters, on behalf of the Winters family.

articles.text: Speakers included Buffy Wicks, Jon Wizard, Andy Madeira A virtual community workshop entitled “Doing Our Part: Affordable Housing in Piedmont” organized by the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) with the League of Women Voters of Piedmont (LWVP) was held on November 9 and included a panel of expert speakers. “When you look at the housing crisis in California, the statistics are pretty alarming,” said Buffy Wicks, Piedmont representative in the State Assembly. In providing introductory remarks, she said, “We are 49 out of 50 [in the country] in homeownership, and fewest homes per population. There is a real shortage of homes at all income levels.” Wicks, who represents the 15th Assembly District, said that those who cannot afford properties or rentals in the Bay Area are forced to commute two or more hours from cities as far away as Stockton. “There are teachers in Oakland Unified School District that are Uber drivers on the side so they can afford housing. That is a big challenge. We’re creating a society of the haves and have-nots, and are squeezing out our middle class,” she said. Wicks described recent state legislation (Senate Bills 9 and 10) aimed at easing the burden of affordable home ownership, which would affect Piedmont and its housing stock. “One of the challenges for Piedmont is there isn’t a ton of vacant [land] waiting to be developed,” she said. “[The city] will have to get creative in terms of how you use these bills we’ve passed recently.” Jon Wizard, a member of the City Council in Seaside and Policy Director for YIMBY Law, offered background information on the Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) and how it affects the state and Piedmont. He explained that cities are required to perform public outreach in the form of surveys, workshops, webinars, and advisory committees; most Bay Area cities and Los Angeles are currently at this stage of the Housing Element process. “Once [a city’s] planning staff gets feedback from the community, they need to work on creating the various policies that will shape the housing element, and the programs within those policies,” he said. “If a city does not have enough vacant land, then it must complete a re-zoning program.” Bay Area city housing elements are due in approximately 13 months, “about enough time to complete [the required] public outreach and create a draft plan,” Wizard said. Andy Madeira, CEO of East Bay Asian Local Development Corporation, described how the economic breakdown of the RHNA new housing unit goal will look. Madeira has been a Piedmont resident for 20 years and has worked in affordable housing for 30 years. “When we moved to Piedmont, it was pretty clear to me that Piedmont is a very homogenous city. It was, and still is, predominately white. I have to say that I’m ashamed I never questioned that, or asked why that was, or what I could do to change that,” he said. Madeira credited the PREC organization for shedding light on affordable housing issues in the community, and said that he hopes people will see that “we can develop a community [in Piedmont] that is welcoming to everyone.” The very low-income level and low-income level appropriate housing units that Piedmont must accommodate accounts for roughly 200 units combined, he explained. Very-low income is defined as an individual who makes less than $48,000 a year. A person earning less than $76,000 a year would be defined as low income. The average income of Piedmont residents is $101,794 a year, and the median household income in Piedmont is $212,222. Madeira used these statistics to explain that currently a verylow or low-income individual cannot afford to rent in Piedmont. He pointed to a sample size of 11 rentals in the city that ranged from $2,200 to $7,500. “Without subsidies, we won’t be able to get new housing units in Piedmont that are affordable. Affordable housing is really housing that is restricted to low income residents in exchange for receiving a variety of different subsidies,” he said. County Measure A-1 funds of $2 million is considered a subsidiary source for Piedmont. The November 9 workshop was initiated by the two organizations as the city updates its Housing Element. PREC member Sarah Karlinsky described it as a critical opportunity for Piedmont to address issues of racial segregation, and to build a more inclusive community. The participatory workshop allowed those who tuned in to join smaller groups to discuss their concerns and wishes regarding affordable housing in Piedmont.
articles.title: LWV, PREC co-host discussion on fair housing in Piedmont

pages.text: 30 Wednesday, November 17, 2021 LWV, PREC co-host discussion on fair housing in Piedmont Speakers included Buffy Wicks, Jon Wizard, Andy Madeira By Allyson Aleksey A virtual community workshop entitled “Doing Our Part: Affordable Housing in Piedmont” organized by the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) with the League of Women Voters of Piedmont (LWVP) was held on November 9 and included a panel of expert speakers. “When you look at the housing crisis in California, the statistics are pretty alarming,” said Buffy Wicks, Piedmont representative in the State Assembly. In providing introductory remarks, she said, “We are 49 out of 50 [in the country] in homeownership, and fewest homes per population. There is a real shortage of homes at all income levels.” Wicks, who represents the 15th Assembly District, said that those who cannot afford properties or rentals in the Bay Area are forced to commute two or more hours from cities as far away as Stockton. “There are teachers in Oakland Unified School District that are Uber drivers on the side so they can afford housing. That is a big challenge. We’re creating a society of the haves and have-nots, and are squeezing out our middle class,” she said. Wicks described recent state legislation (Senate Bills 9 and 10) aimed at easing the burden of affordable home ownership, which would affect Piedmont and its housing stock. “One of the challenges for Piedmont is there isn’t a ton of vacant [land] waiting to be developed,” she said. “[The city] will have to get creative in terms of how you use these bills we’ve passed recently.” Jon Wizard, a member of the City Council in Seaside and Policy Director for YIMBY Law, offered background information on the Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) and how it affects the state and Piedmont. He explained that cities are required to perform public outreach in the form of surveys, workshops, webinars, and advisory committees; most Bay Area cities and Los Angeles are currently at this stage of the Housing Element process. “Once [a city’s] planning staff gets feedback from the community, they need to work on creating the various policies that will shape the housing element, and the programs within those policies,” he said. “If a city does not have enough vacant land, then it must complete a re-zoning program.” Bay Area city housing elements are due in approximately 13 months, “about enough time to complete [the required] public outreach and create a draft plan,” Wizard said. Andy Madeira, CEO of East Bay Asian Local Development Corporation, described how the economic breakdown of the RHNA new housing unit goal will look. Madeira has been a Piedmont resident for 20 years and has worked in affordable housing for 30 years. “When we moved to Piedmont, it was pretty clear to me that Piedmont is a very homogenous city. It was, and still is, predominately white. I have to say that I’m ashamed I never questioned that, or asked why that was, or what I could do to change that,” he said. Madeira credited the PREC organization for shedding light on affordable housing issues in the community, and said that he hopes people will see that “we can develop a community [in Piedmont] that is welcoming to everyone.” The very low-income level and low-income level appropriate housing units that Piedmont must accommodate accounts for roughly 200 units combined, he explained. Very-low income is defined as an individual who makes less than $48,000 a year. A person earning less than $76,000 a year would be defined as low income. The average income of Piedmont residents is $101,794 a year, and the median household income in Piedmont is $212,222. Madeira used these statistics to explain that currently a verylow or low-income individual cannot afford to rent in Piedmont. He pointed to a sample size of 11 rentals in the city that ranged from $2,200 to $7,500. “Without subsidies, we won’t be able to get new housing units in Piedmont that are affordable. Affordable housing is really housing that is restricted to low income residents in exchange for receiving a variety of different subsidies,” he said. County Measure A-1 funds of $2 million is considered a subsidiary source for Piedmont. The November 9 workshop was initiated by the two organizations as the city updates its Housing Element. PREC member Sarah Karlinsky described it as a critical opportunity for Piedmont to address issues of racial segregation, and to build a more inclusive community. The participatory workshop allowed those who tuned in to join smaller groups to discuss their concerns and wishes regarding affordable housing in Piedmont. The Luxor Obelisk is one of a pair presented by the Sultan of Egypt in 1830 to the King of France for gratitude in deciphering the hieroglyphs of Champollion. I imagine les femmes dressed in jewels and rustling silks and flushed by the whirling dances at a royal ball where they were squired by French nobility. We mortals pause before the majesty of Place de la Concorde, its central Obelisk flanked by two fountains, one dedicated to the rivers, the other to the sea. We gaze across the Seine to the south with a clear view of the Eiffel Tower and beyond. The Luxor Obelisk is one of a pair presented by the Sultan of Egypt in 1830 to the King of France for gratitude in deciphering the hieroglyphs of Champollion. Each of the two matching stone pillars is 75 feet tall, weighs 220 tons, and dates from the 13th century B.C. under the reign of Pharaoh Rhamses II. One obelisk was transported from Thebes temple ruins to Alexandria to Paris, a journey that took six years of planning and execution. Not until 1981 did France under President François Mitterrand make an official overture to Egypt to decline the second obelisk. The year 1789 changed much about King Louis XVI’s reign, including his beheading and that of his queen consort Marie Antoinette in 1793 under the Reign of Terror when 17,000 executions took place. The area was renamed Place de la Révolution during the upheaval. Despite the loss of the French monarchy, followed by the heady rise but stunning defeat of Napoleon, the French had three consecutive kings until the Revolution of 1848 brought forth the Second French Republic and a presidential election. The aristocrat Louis Napoleon, nephew to Napoleon Bonaparte was the outsized winner and president until 1852. He crowned himself, as did his famous uncle, Emperor Napoleon III, and he reigned until 1870, the last French royal.
